question: During an incident, every target in an ALB target group starts failing its health checks — yet requests keep flowing to the broken targets and the "traffic is being served" dashboard stays green. What ALB behavior explains this, and what is the monitoring lesson?
choices: Connection draining: existing connections are allowed to finish for deregistration_delay (default 300s), so traffic tails off slowly rather than stopping

Fail-open: when every target in a group is unhealthy, the ALB routes to all of them anyway — a struggling target beats no target — so request volume is not proof of health; alarm on UnHealthyHostCount instead
Cross-zone load balancing: the load balancer nodes redistribute traffic to healthy targets in other Availability Zones, keeping total request volume constant
Health checks only gate the registration of new targets; targets already registered keep receiving traffic regardless of their check results
explanation: The ALB fails open: health checks normally pull a failing target out of rotation, but when the entire group is unhealthy there is nothing left to prefer, so the ALB deliberately routes to all targets — a degraded backend may still serve some requests, while routing to nothing serves none. The operational consequence is that "requests are flowing" can be true while every backend is broken, so dashboards must alarm on health-check state (UnHealthyHostCount) and error rates, never on traffic volume. Draining applies to targets being deliberately deregistered, cross-zone balancing only helps if healthy targets exist somewhere, and under normal conditions health checks absolutely do gate routing for registered targets.

question: A team deploys a new version by deregistering the old ECS tasks from the ALB target group and stopping them immediately. Users report dropped connections and 502s during every deploy — yet health checks stay green throughout. Which mechanism did the team bypass, and what is the graceful pattern?
choices: The health-check interval (30 s) times the unhealthy threshold (2) means the ALB needs up to a minute to notice a stopped task and keeps routing to it; lowering the interval to 5 s and the threshold to 1 makes deploys near-seamless without other changes

Deregistration puts a target into a draining state: the ALB stops sending it new requests but lets in-flight ones finish, for up to deregistration_delay (default 300 s). Stopping the process immediately kills exactly those live connections — the draining window exists so old tasks can finish the work they hold. Graceful deploys stop a target only after draining completes; the lesson is that shutdown is a two-phase act — stop accepting new work, then finish the work in hand

With cross-zone load balancing enabled (the ALB default), every node routes to every target, so a deregistered task keeps receiving requests from nodes in other zones until their target lists converge; disabling cross-zone makes deregistration take effect zone-locally and instantly

Clients cache the ALB's DNS record for its 60-second TTL, so requests keep arriving at node IPs that still hold connections to the old tasks; fronting the ALB with a Route 53 alias record eliminates the client-side caching window
explanation: The failure sits at the connection-lifecycle layer, not the health layer. Health checks answer 'should NEW requests go to this target?' — they say nothing about requests already in flight. Deregistration likewise governs new traffic, and provides deregistration_delay precisely so the old traffic can complete: that is connection draining, the mechanism that makes rolling deploys invisible to users. Killing the process the moment deregistration starts turns every in-flight request into a reset connection, and no health-check tuning can help because health was never the problem — the green checks throughout were the tell. Orchestrators like ECS honour the draining window automatically; deregister-then-kill by hand re-creates the failure. The distractors blame real mechanisms for the wrong failure: faster health checks only shrink detection time for targets that fail, which these didn't; cross-zone balancing changes which nodes route to which targets, but draining state applies across all nodes either way; and DNS TTL governs how clients find ALB nodes, not how the ALB manages its own server-side connections to targets.

question: A service serves traffic on port 8080 and exposes its probe endpoint on a separate management port 8081, so the target group's health check is configured for port 8081 and path /health. Every target is marked unhealthy, yet from a bastion host inside the VPC `curl http://<target-private-ip>:8081/health` returns 200 instantly. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The ALB health-checks targets from outside the VPC, so a target with only a private IP cannot be probed; the targets need public IPs or an egress path back to the load balancer's public nodes
A health check can only use the port the target is registered with; ELB silently ignores a port override, probes 8080 with the path /health, gets a 404, and marks the target unhealthy

A health check is an ordinary connection originating from the load balancer nodes, so the ALB's security group must allow outbound to 8081 and the target's security group must allow inbound on 8081 from the ALB — a rule set written for the traffic port only leaves the probe blocked and timing out

With the healthy threshold at 5 and a 30-second interval, targets need about 150 seconds of passing probes before they leave the initial state; the group was inspected too early and would have gone healthy on its own
explanation: The bastion test is the decisive evidence: the endpoint works, so the application is not the problem — reachability from the load balancer is. Health checks are not a side channel or an out-of-band signal; they are real network connections opened by the ALB nodes to the target, and therefore subject to exactly the same firewall rules as request traffic. Splitting the probe onto a second port doubles the set of paths that must be opened, and security-group rules authored around the traffic port alone leave that second path closed, so the probe times out and the target is pulled from service. The engineering lesson generalises: any port you configure — traffic, probe, or admin — is a port you must also authorise, and connectivity should be verified from the caller's position, not from a host that happens to have different permissions. Of the alternatives, the ALB reaches targets over private IPs from inside the VPC, so no public addressing is involved; a health check port override is honoured, not ignored; and the threshold delay would resolve itself with time and would not hold every target unhealthy indefinitely.

question: One ALB fronts a marketing site and an API. The HTTPS listener has rule priority 1 = host-header `example.com` → web target group, priority 2 = path-pattern `/api/*` → api target group. Requests to `https://example.com/api/orders` all land on the web target group and return 404. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Listener rules are evaluated most-specific-first, so a path condition should outrank a bare host condition; the API rule loses because path-pattern has lower intrinsic precedence than host-header in ELB's matching order

Rule evaluation stops at the first rule whose conditions all match, in ascending priority order — priority 1 matches every request for that host, so priority 2 is never reached. The specific case must sit at the lower priority number, matching host and path together in one rule; the broad rule then acts as the catch-all
`/api/*` does not match `/api/orders` because the wildcard only covers a single additional path segment; adding a second pattern `/api/*/*` makes the rule match and take effect
A rule's conditions are combined across rules, not within one, so the host and path conditions must be split into two rules to be ANDed; both are currently being ORed against the same target group
explanation: The routing model is first-match-wins over an ordered list, not best-match over a set: the listener walks its rules by ascending priority, applies the first whose conditions all hold, and never looks further, with the mandatory default rule as the final fallback. A rule whose only condition is a host header matches every request for that host, including the API paths, so placing it at priority 1 shadows everything below it. That makes rule ordering a design responsibility exactly like ordering the branches of a conditional or the entries of a firewall list: the narrow cases go first, the broad case last. The fix is to match host and path together in the higher-priority rule — conditions within one rule are ANDed — leaving the host-only rule to absorb the remainder. The distractors invert the model (ELB does not rank conditions by specificity or type), misstate path-pattern matching (`*` spans any number of characters, so `/api/*` matches `/api/orders`), and misplace the AND boundary, which lives inside a rule, not across rules.

question: An ALB terminates TLS on HTTPS:443 and forwards to targets over HTTP. The application framework has a "force HTTPS" feature enabled that issues a 301 to the https:// form of the URL whenever the incoming request is not encrypted. Browsers now report a redirect loop on every page, even though the address bar shows https. What is the root cause and the right fix?
choices: The HTTP:80 listener's redirect rule is bouncing requests to itself because its action does not override the port; deleting the HTTP:80 listener stops the loop
The ALB is not forwarding the original Host header, so the framework rebuilds the redirect against the load balancer's own DNS name and the client is sent back through the same listener repeatedly
The ACM certificate on the listener covers only the apex domain, so requests for the www host fail validation and the ALB emits a canonical redirect on each attempt

TLS terminates at the load balancer, so the target's connection is genuinely plain HTTP and always will be: the app sees an unencrypted request, redirects to https, the ALB decrypts the new request and forwards plain HTTP again, forever. The application must infer the client's original scheme from the proxy's forwarded headers (X-Forwarded-Proto) rather than from its own socket — or leave the redirect entirely to the ALB's HTTP:80 rule and disable it in the app
explanation: Terminating TLS moves a fact out of the application's reach. Once the ALB decrypts the front-end connection, the request the target receives is plain HTTP by design, so any code that decides "was this secure?" by inspecting its own connection will answer no on every request — including the one that just arrived over HTTPS — and redirect endlessly. The general principle is that behind a reverse proxy the application must treat client-facing properties (scheme, client IP, original host) as proxy-supplied metadata carried in X-Forwarded-* headers, not as properties of the socket it is reading; frameworks expose this as a "trust proxy" setting. The cleaner alternative is to stop duplicating the concern: the ALB's HTTP:80 listener already performs the http→https redirect at the edge, so the app-level force-HTTPS can simply be turned off. The distractors each blame a real but different mechanism: an ALB redirect action defaults to preserving the original components and is a well-worn pattern rather than a self-loop, deleting the HTTP listener would not stop a loop that occurs on HTTPS requests; the ALB does pass the Host header through to targets; and a certificate that does not cover a hostname produces a TLS warning at handshake time, not an application-level redirect.
